newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa sees bias in arms row, awaits U.S. visit.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa sees bias in arms row, awaits U.S. visit.

text.p: Defence Minister Joe Modise upheld South Africa's right to sell arms to Syria on Friday, accusing critics of the proposed deal of a pro-Israel bias.
Modise, speaking ahead of the scheduled arrival in the country of U.S. Vice-President Al Gore later on Friday, also reaffirmed South Africa's warm relations with Iran.

The defence minister's remarks at a briefing to reporters and diplomats at parliament in Cape Town appeared likely to offend the United States, which is a warm supporter of Israel and classes both Iran and Syria as terrorist states.
Washington warned South Africa in January it would cut aid if a proposed contract to sell South African tank targetting gear to Syria was finalised.

"As far as we are concerned, we treat all states equally. I've never heard the same questions asked about Syria or Lebanon, when arms are being sold to Israel," Modise said when asked about the deal, particularly its impact on Israel.
"I've never heard anybody ask whether the countries selling equipment to Israel concerned themselves with the feelings of the neighbours."
Modise, who has previously compared Israel's treatment of Palestinians with apartheid, said many "important" countries sold arms to Israel.
"No thought is given to the Palestinians and their sufferings...Why does it become such a big problem when the other side (Syria) is now also being equipped?" he asked.

Asked about a reported agreement under which Iranian submarines would be allowed to use Mozambican harbours -- denied by Maputo earlier this week -- Modise said South Africa would not dictate to either country.
"Iran is a country which has relations with South Africa," he said. "We have seen no hostile act from Iran, in fact it's the opposite. Relations between Iran and South Africa are very friendly...
"We will continue strengthening relations between ourselves and Mozambique, also with Iran, so as to sleep comfortably at night and not worry about submarines," Modise said.

Modise and his deputy minister, Ronnie Kasrils, said both Mozambique and Tanzania had asked South Africa to use its navy to protect their waters from being plundered by foreign fishing fleets, but South Africa's navy did not have the necessary ships.
"Our neighbours are going to look further afield, east, west, whatever direction, and welcome those who are able to come to their assistance," Kasrils said.
The defence ministry is trying to persuade the government to approve the purchase of four Corvettes and several submarines, but are meeting resistance because of the costs.
Gore is expected in the Indian Ocean port of Durban on Friday night.
He is expected in Cape Town on Saturday for talks with Deputy President Thabo Mbeki on a range of farm, trade, tax and other issues being handled by a binational commission.
United States and South African officials have said the Syrian arms row is not on the official agenda.
